transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Corva Coleman.
Israel is pressing on with a military raid in the occupied West Bank,
displacing thousands of Palestinians from their homes.
NPR's Daniel Estrin reports from Tel Aviv this comes ahead of Israeli elections tomorrow.
Israel launched the offensive after Palestinian gunmen killed two Israeli soldiers
at a military checkpoint in the West Bank three days ago.
The city's mayor, Yusuf Jabari, tells NPR that Israel is targeting a wide radius
of neighborhoods near where the gunmen came from in the city of Hebron.
He says some 3,000 people have been displaced from their homes in the offensive,
including elderly and children.
He says water and sewage infrastructure has been destroyed.
And he says the city is on lockdown, with Palestinians not leaving their homes
and Israeli military vehicles roaming the streets.
The Palestinian mayor accuses Israel's leadership of collective punishment
in a bid to gain right-wing Israelis' votes in elections Tuesday.
Daniel Estrin, NPR News, Tel Aviv.
Brazilians have voted to return incumbent President Luis Anasio Lula de Silva to office.
He defeated challenger Flavio Bolsonaro by more than 4 million votes.
And Piers Karikán reports Bolsonaro is refusing to accept the result.
Polls had predicted Lula, who turns 81 Tuesday, would lose to conservative Flavio Bolsonaro.
The 45-year-old senator is the son of Lula's chief rival, former President Jair Bolsonaro,
who's serving a 27-year sentence for plotting a coup.
Speaking to supporters last night, a horse Lula thanked Brazilians.
Thanks to the generosity of the Brazilian youth who took to the streets to defend democracy, he said.
But Bolsonaro is questioning a Supreme Court ruling that allowed polls to stay open two additional hours
and said the justice who ordered the extension, quote, "changed the rules" in the middle of the game.
Karikán, NPR News, Brasilia.
In Alaska, Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola is recovering from injuries she sustained in a weekend car crash.
From Alaska, public media Liz Ruskin reports Peltola is trying to unseat Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan.
Anchorage police say Peltola and family members were taken to the hospital Saturday after another vehicle rear-ended theirs.
Her campaign says she has minor injuries and will be back on the trail Tuesday.
A spokesperson says there's no reason to believe the collision was politically motivated.
Meanwhile, her attorneys are asking a judge to quickly dismiss a Justice Department lawsuit
it seeks to block the state from certifying the election if Sullivan narrowly loses,
pending an investigation to see if voters were confused by a second Dan Sullivan on the ballot.
The senator is listed on the ballot as the Republican incumbent.
For NPR News, I'm Liz Ruskin in Anchorage.
You're listening to NPR News.
President Trump will campaign in Mississippi later today for Republican candidates.
He did that over the weekend in Michigan and Ohio.
So did former President Barack Obama, who stumped for Democratic candidates.
A.I. company Anthropic is preparing for its initial public offering.
It released paperwork today indicating it will try to sell stock to the public as soon as possible.
It will seek to raise billions of dollars.
Students are still missing more school than before the pandemic.
Chronic absenteeism occurs when students miss more than 10 percent of the school year.
And Piers Janaki Mehta has more on the latest.
We'll start with the good news.
More students have been coming to school regularly in the last few years.
But attendance still isn't where it was before the pandemic.
That's all in a new report from five organizations that focus on chronic absenteeism.
And the reasons for absences have changed.
For example, families are more cautious about sickness since COVID. Recent immigration crackdowns have led some parents to keep their kids at home.
And students also report feeling less connected when they're at school.
Building strong relationships with students, making class more engaging,
and making sure there's reliable transportation are among some of the strategies schools can use to keep improving attendance.
Janaki Mehta, NPR News.
There are flood warnings still posted for the Four Corners area in the southwest. That's Arizona, Colorado, New Mexico and Utah.
The National Weather Service says there has been catastrophic flooding along the San Juan River.
I'm Corva Coleman, NPR News in Washington.
And get NPR+ at plus.npr.org. That's plus.npr.org.

topics.text: Israel presses military raid in occupied West Bank city of Hebron, displacing about 3,000 Palestinians
Brazil's Lula defeats Flavio Bolsonaro by over 4 million votes; Bolsonaro refuses to accept result
Alaska Senate candidate Mary Peltola recovering from minor injuries after weekend car crash in Anchorage
Justice Department lawsuit seeks to block Alaska from certifying Senate election over second Dan Sullivan on ballot
Trump to campaign in Mississippi for Republican candidates, following weekend stops in Michigan and Ohio
Former President Obama stumped for Democratic candidates over the weekend
AI company Anthropic files paperwork preparing for initial public offering to raise billions
Report finds chronic student absenteeism still above pre-pandemic levels, citing caution, immigration crackdowns, and disconnection
Flood warnings remain for Four Corners region after catastrophic flooding along San Juan River
